depth.h2: What Arlington Heights Homes Need From a Plumber
depth.intro: The median home in Arlington Heights was built in 1974, and about 3 in 4 went up between 1940 and 1989. That postwar building boom, plus mature trees and long Cook County winters, shapes the problems we see most.

tiles.title: Postwar Homes, Older Pipes
tiles.body: More than a third of Arlington Heights homes were built between 1940 and 1969. Many still have their original clay sewer line, cast iron drains or galvanized water pipe. Tree roots work their way into clay pipe at the joints, and galvanized pipe rusts from the inside until water pressure drops. A [camera inspection](/arlington-heights/video-camera-sewer-inspections) shows the condition of your sewer line before you decide on a [sewer repair](/arlington-heights/sewer-repair).

tiles.title: Heavy Rain, Sump Pumps and Catch Basins
tiles.body: Heavy spring rain and snowmelt put basements across the area to the test. A [sump pump with a battery backup](/arlington-heights/sump-pumps) keeps running when the power goes out. A [backflow valve](/arlington-heights/flood-control-maintenance) stops sewage from coming up through floor drains. Outside, a [catch basin](/arlington-heights/catch-basin) that’s full of leaves and silt can send water right back toward your foundation.

tiles.title: 1970s and 1980s Homes Showing Their Age
tiles.body: Another 4 in 10 homes went up in the 1970s and 1980s, and they’re now 37 to 56 years old. Original shut-off valves, supply lines and drain pipes are wearing out, and many homes are on their second or third water heater. A [small leak](/arlington-heights/leak-repairs) or a [water heater that runs out too fast](/arlington-heights/water-heater-repair) is often the first sign. A [whole-home checkup](/arlington-heights/plumbing-maintenance) shows what needs attention before it fails.

tiles.title: Winter Freezes and Burst Pipes
tiles.body: Northwest suburban winters bring weeks of below-freezing nights. Pipes in exterior walls, unheated garages and crawl spaces freeze first, along with the line that feeds your outdoor spigot. When one splits, the leak usually shows up once it thaws. Know where your main shut-off valve is, and call us 24/7 if a [pipe bursts](/arlington-heights/burst-pipe-repair).

faq.h2: Plumbing Questions From Arlington Heights Homeowners

items.q: How much does a plumber cost in Arlington Heights?
items.a: It depends on the job. The main factors are what’s wrong, how hard it is to reach, the parts or materials needed and the age of your plumbing. A 1950s home with clay sewer pipe can take more work to repair the right way than a newer one. We give you a flat-rate price before any work begins, so you know the cost going in. Give us a call and we’ll walk you through it.

items.q: How fast can you get to my home in an emergency?
items.preview: Call us any time, day or night, including weekends and holidays.
items.a: Call us any time, day or night, including weekends and holidays. Our East Central Road office keeps our plumbers close to Arlington Heights, and we [treat emergencies as a priority](/arlington-heights/emergency-plumbing). Arrival times depend on the day, but we’ll get a plumber to you as soon as we can.

items.q: My home was built in the 1950s or 1960s. Is it at higher risk?
items.preview: It can be. More than a third of Arlington Heights homes were built between 1940 and 1969.
items.a: It can be. More than a third of Arlington Heights homes were built between 1940 and 1969. Homes from those years often have clay sewer pipe, cast iron drains or galvanized water lines, and all of them wear out with age. Age alone doesn’t mean something is wrong. A [camera inspection](/arlington-heights/video-camera-sewer-inspections) tells you where your sewer line stands, so you can plan a repair instead of reacting to a backup.

items.q: How often should I replace my sump pump?
items.preview: Most sump pumps last somewhere around 7 to 10 years, and less if they run often.
items.a: Most sump pumps last somewhere around 7 to 10 years, and less if they run often. Test yours before the spring rains: pour a bucket of water into the pit and watch it turn on and shut off. A loud motor, a pump that runs nonstop or one that won’t kick on are all signs it’s time for a [replacement](/arlington-heights/sump-pumps). Adding a battery backup keeps it running when the power goes out.

items.q: What does a catch basin do, and why does mine back up?
items.preview: A catch basin collects rainwater from your yard or driveway and sends it into the storm drain.
items.a: A catch basin collects rainwater from your yard or driveway and sends it into the storm drain. Leaves, silt and debris build up in the bottom over time, and when it fills, water pools in the yard or flows back toward the house. Regular [cleaning or repair](/arlington-heights/catch-basin) keeps it draining the way it should.

items.q: How do I protect my basement from sewer backups?
items.preview: Start with three things: a backflow valve on your sewer line, a sump pump with a battery backup, and a regular check of your sewer line for roots and debris.
items.a: Start with three things: a backflow valve on your sewer line, a sump pump with a battery backup, and a regular check of your sewer line for roots and debris. For homes with repeat backups, an [overhead sewer system](/arlington-heights/overhead-sewer-systems) lifts basement wastewater above the level where backups happen. We can look at your setup and tell you which option makes sense for your home.
